name: Mexico City subsidence

focus.label: Tláhuac and Valle de Chalco, 14 km across

signal.label: Sinking rate (negative = away from the satellite)
signal.positive: toward the satellite (rising); negative = sinking, along the line of sight, so true vertical sinking is a little more
signal.noise_method: robust scatter of differences between neighbouring measured cells (includes real gradients)

zero.method: median rate over the highest 15% of the terrain (dem >= p85)
zero.meaning: signal = (los / 10 / years) minus offset_cm_yr; years = pair[1] - pair[0] in days / 365.25

line.name: the edge of the sinking ground
line.raster_unit: per year (tilt: change in sinking rate per metre; 1 in N a year with N = 1 / (count * raster_scale))
line.measured_means: the sinking rate changes faster across the edge than the noise on stable ground (tilt above 1 in 5,600 a year)
line.dashed_means: the edge is there (the ground passes the -5 cm a year mark) but the rate changes too gently across it for the radar to tell from noise
line.caveat: Not a crack or a fault: the contour where the smoothed sinking rate reaches 5 cm a year relative to stable ground. The sharp bend near the Tláhuac story is short (about 1 km); most of the contour is gentle (dashed). Rates are zeroed on the highest 15% of the terrain, which leaves the Sierra de Santa Catarina reading about +2 cm a year, so the zero is uncertain by about 2 cm a year. Solid rings around cinder cones are probably steep-slope artifacts, not sinking. Contours shorter than 4 km with less than 0.5 km of solid line were dropped as noise. Motion is along the radar's slanted view.
